title: RPG: Repository Planning Graph for Unified Code Generation
one_liner: Instead of free-form writing, generate complete code repositories by first building an explicit graph of what to build and how pieces connect.
lead: Large language models can write individual functions well, but writing an entire code repository from scratch remains difficult. The core problem: models rely on natural language planning, which is vague and leaves room for misaligned parts. This paper introduces a Repository Planning Graph (RPG), a structured blueprint that maps out all the files, data flows, and dependencies before any code is written. By planning as a graph first, then generating code guided by that plan, the method generates far larger, more complete repositories with fewer errors.

problem.h2: Repositories are too complex for word-by-word generation
paras: When a model writes code file by file, it forgets what files already exist, loses track of what data each piece expects, and builds incompatible parts. A naive approach is to tell the model the entire specification in words and hope it stays consistent — but thousands of details get lost or twisted because natural language is inherently ambiguous.

The real world has file structures (some files import others), data types (functions expect inputs in specific formats), and dependencies (module A needs module B). A model that ignores these relationships produces broken code that does not run together, even if each file looks reasonable in isolation.

callout.html: The paper replaces vague word-based planning with an explicit graph that shows all files, data flows, and function signatures, then uses that graph to guide code generation.

steps.b: Proposal stage: what features to build
steps.text: High-level planning decides which files and modules the repository needs.
Build a graph where nodes are files and functions, edges show dependencies and data types.
For each node, generate the function or file, constrained by the graph structure.
Write the actual code, run tests to catch mismatches, fix broken imports or type errors.
When a test fails, the graph shows which nodes (files and functions) are involved, so repairs touch only the relevant code without accidentally breaking unrelated parts.

object.h2: The single change: explicit structure instead of prose
paras: Instead of describing the repository in natural language and hoping the model infers the structure, the paper builds an explicit graph before any code is written. The graph encodes which files exist, what functions each contains, what data types flow between functions, and how files depend on each other. Code generation then follows this blueprint rather than inventing structure on the fly.

hidden.name: graph consistency score
paras: The paper measures how well the generated code matches the planned graph structure. A high score means functions have the right signatures, imports are correct, and data types flow as expected. Low scores reveal mismatches: a function that returns the wrong type, or a file importing something that does not exist.
The paper estimates this by checking whether test cases pass — tests fail when the code structure is wrong, so test accuracy directly reflects how closely the code followed the graph blueprint.

heat.caption: Darker means higher structural integrity (correct files, correct types, tests pass).

reads.html: Structural clarity is how well all the pieces fit together without errors. High clarity means the model knew exactly what to build and how it all connects.
Test accuracy (69.7%) and coverage (81.5%) are direct measures of how well the generated code matched the planned graph structure.

mechanism.h2: Why the graph fixes the problem
paras: A model writing code line by line has no memory of earlier files and no way to plan ahead. When it writes file 3, it has no record of what file 1 exported, so it guesses. When it writes a function, it does not know if the caller will pass the right type. The result is mismatched types, missing imports, and unused code.

The graph solves this by making all relationships explicit BEFORE code is written. Once the model has a graph showing that file A calls function foo from file B, and foo expects an integer, the code generation stage is constrained — it must write file A in a way that calls foo correctly, and it must write foo to accept an integer. The model no longer guesses. Additionally, when a test fails, the graph tells the localization step exactly which files are involved in that test, so repairs are fast and do not break unrelated code.

stages.s: Plan which files and modules exist
Generate code guided by graph structure
Test and repair broken imports or type mismatches

math.words: For each function signature mismatch, subtract a penalty. For each correct import and data flow, add credit. The total is how closely the code followed the graph.
symbols: count of functions with the right input and output types
count of imports that match what the graph showed
count of data values flowing between functions as planned
total number of functions in the graph

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: A small repo has 10 functions and 5 imports.
Generated code: 9 functions have correct signatures, 4 imports are correct, 8 data flows match the plan.
Consistency = (9 + 4 + 8) / (10 + 5) * 100 = 21 / 15 * 100 = 140 / 100 = does not work this way.
Better: count correct elements = 9 + 4 + 8 = 21 right elements. Total possible = 10 + 5 + 12 (data flows) = 27. Score = 21/27 = 77.8% consistency.
If tests pass, consistency is high. If tests fail on import errors, consistency is low because the code did not follow the graph.

math.note: Consistency is measured by how many tests pass — tests fail when signatures, imports, or data types do not match the graph.

charts.title: Word-by-word generation (naive baseline)
charts.note: Without a graph, the model generates sparse, broken code and misses many files.

charts.title: With Repository Planning Graph
charts.note: The graph guides generation toward complete, testable systems. Nearly 3.9 times more code, and tests actually pass.

items.html: If the planning stage builds a graph that is missing files or has the wrong data types, the code generation stage will faithfully build the wrong thing, because the generator follows the graph structure as a blueprint. A bad graph leads to bad code because there is no other source of truth for how pieces should connect. The model must correctly understand the task during planning.

items.b: Code does not match the graph structure.
items.html: Even with a good graph, the generation stage might ignore it and write code that violates the graph. Tests catch this, but fixing requires re-running the entire generation, not just patching one file.
If file A imports file B which imports file A, the system cannot generate either correctly. The planning stage must avoid building cycles.

items.b: Done right: graph is precise, generation respects it, tests validate.
items.html: When the planning stage builds an accurate graph (all files, correct types, no cycles), and the generation stage follows it, and tests run successfully, the result is a large, integrated repository that works.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small task (e.g., a to-do app) where you specify the high-level features: a database handler, an API server, and a command-line interface. Have the model plan the graph (which files exist, what each function does, what types flow between them). Then have the model generate the full code. Finally, run the test suite (or write simple tests that check each file can be imported, each function has the right signature, and basic operations work).
Measure how many lines were generated, how many tests pass, and how many of the required features are present. Compare to a baseline that generates code without building the graph first.
demo.closing: The demo must show that explicit graph planning generates far more code, with far fewer broken imports and type errors, than models that write without a plan.
